newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam steps up security ahead of national polls.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam steps up security ahead of national polls.

text.p: Vietnam's communist government called for heightened security on Thursday ahead of Sunday's parliamentary polls.
State-media said soldiers, police and municipal authorities were reinforcing measures aimed at ensuring social order and security.
Newspapers also carried a message from the National Assembly's standing board calling for "active participation" by all members of the public and army in the elections.

Voting for a new 450-seat National Assembly is due to start early on Sunday. More than 660 state-approved candidates are taking part, 112 of whom are independents from outside the ruling Communist Party.
There was no indication that the authorities were concerned about any specific threat to public order.
The last election, in 1992, was marked in Hanoi by a rare protest when a man flung leaflets criticising the event as a farce from the second floor of a city centre market building.
Vietnam's elections defy comparison with polls in most other countries.
There is no opposition taking part, but voter turnout is normally declared close to 100 percent, despite evidence that many people get friends or family members to vote on their behalf.
The National Assembly, which meets twice each year, has traditionally been viewed as a rubber-stamp legislature with few powers.
But analysts say that is no longer the case, and point to recent debates among members as evidence that it is flexing new-found muscle.
